faq.q: How does an arch bridge work?
faq.a: The curved arch carries loads as compression, squeezing its stones together, and passes the push down and outward into strong supports at each end called abutments.
The keystone is the wedge at the top of a stone arch, placed last. It locks the two halves together, but every stone matters, because the load is shared all round the curve.
asks: Is the keystone the most important stone?

faq.q: What is thrust in an arch?
faq.a: Thrust is the outward push at the ends of an arch. The flatter the arch, the bigger the sideways thrust, so flat arches need very strong abutments.
Abutments are the heavy supports at each end of an arch that resist its thrust. They are often built into solid rock or the sides of a valley.
asks: What holds the ends of an arch?

faq.a: Builders first made a temporary wooden frame called centring, laid the stones over it and set the keystone last. Once complete, the arch held itself up and the frame was removed.
asks: How did the Romans build arches?

facts: Many Roman stone arch structures still stand after nearly 2,000 years, including the Pont du Gard aqueduct bridge in France.
A flatter arch pushes outward more strongly than a tall, rounded one, so it needs stronger abutments.

quiz.say: What will happen to a stone arch bridge if its abutments slowly slide apart?
quiz.show: If an arch's abutments slide apart…

options.show: The arch sags and can collapse
options.say: The arch sags and can collapse

quiz.why: The abutments hold back the arch's outward thrust. If they move, the arch spreads and sags, its stones lose their squeeze and can drop out.

wrong.1: Spreading lets the stones lose their squeeze, which weakens the arch.
wrong.2: An arch depends on its ends staying put.
